title: Remote Data Storage
summary: Remote data storage is a mitigation that moves logs, backups and sensitive files off the host that produces them and onto a separate system the attacker does not already control. The mechanism is straightforward: endpoints and servers forward telemetry and data over an authenticated channel to a central collector, object store or write-once repository, and local copies are trimmed so they cannot be quietly destroyed. In real environments this looks like a log collector, a security information and event management platform, a cloud bucket with versioning and object lock, or a hardened backup target on its own network segment with its own credentials. Evidence of good practice appears as steady ingest, defined retention and the absence of gaps around the time of an incident, while evidence of failure is silence in the feed from a host that is still running. Misunderstandings cluster in three places: teams treat backups as logging, assume the destination is safe simply because it is remote, and reuse credentials between source and destination so that one stolen secret reaches both copies.

beginner.definition: Remote data storage means keeping important files somewhere other than the computer that created them. The copy lives on a separate server, in a cloud service, or on a protected backup system. If an attacker damages or encrypts the original machine, the other copy is still safe.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many attacks end with the attacker deleting logs or encrypting files to hide the trail and demand money. If the only copy sits on the same machine, it disappears with the machine. Keeping a second copy elsewhere means you can still investigate and still recover. It also protects you when hardware simply fails, which happens far more often than an attack does.
howItWorks: Choose which data must leave the machine, such as security logs, database dumps and business documents.
Send that data over an encrypted channel to a separate server or a cloud service.
Give the storage system its own credentials, different from the accounts used on the source machine.
Make the stored copy read-only or versioned, so nobody can quietly overwrite or delete it.
Limit who can reach the storage system, and keep it on a separate network segment.
Test the restore path regularly, because a backup you cannot restore is not a backup.
beginner.example: Picture a small shop that keeps its only paper ledger on the counter. If a thief takes the ledger, the shop has no record of anything. A careful owner photographs each page at closing time and sends the pictures to a locked cabinet at home. The counter copy is still useful and still at risk, but the shop can always rebuild its records. Remote data storage works the same way: the original stays where people need it, and a protected copy waits somewhere else.
takeaways: Keep at least one copy of important data away from the machine that produced it.
Use separate credentials and separate networks, so one stolen password cannot reach both copies.
Test restoring the data, not just creating the copy.

objectives: Explain why logs and backups stored only on the source host are a single point of failure.
Describe how log forwarding and off-host backup targets are configured in practice.
Identify the credential and network separation that keeps a remote copy out of an attacker's reach.
Summarise how retention, versioning and immutability protect stored evidence.
Outline a restore test and the evidence it produces.
